claims.claim: Justin Alexander says the standardized 3rd Edition adventure format encourages writers to fill the format with text that is not needed.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: it tends to encourage writers to “fill the format”
claims.page: Art of the Key, 'Adventure Formatting Guides'

claims.claim: Justin Alexander labels the dense undifferentiated paragraph key that TSR used for most of a decade the Gygax wall of text.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.page: Art of the Key, 'A Brief History of the Key'

claims.claim: Justin Alexander's prescribed key opens with the information a character perceives on entering, which he calls seen in a glance.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key - Part 2', The Alexandrian, 2014

claims.claim: Justin Alexander's alternative to a fixed key format is to order the entry by the sequence in which information will be wanted at the table.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key - Part 2', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: focus on the sequencing of information

claims.claim: Justin Alexander tells key writers to move from the general to the specific as the players investigate.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key - Part 2', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: move from the general to the specific

claims.claim: Justin Alexander bolds the name of each significant element in a room so the GM can find the matching information quickly.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key - Part 2', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: the bold title makes it easy to find the information

claims.feature: other: background and history in a key
claims.claim: Justin Alexander confines a location's history and former use to a GM Background tag that must be brief and infrequently needed.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key - Part 2', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: It should be brief, to the point, and infrequently needed.

claims.claim: Justin Alexander credits the delve format with the single good idea that everything the GM needs is on the page.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key - Part 3', The Alexandrian, 2016
claims.quote: Everything you need is on the page.

claims.claim: Justin Alexander grants that boxed text virtually guarantees essential information is not accidentally omitted in play.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls', The Alexandrian, 2022
claims.quote: will virtually guarantee that it’s not accidentally omitted

claims.claim: Justin Alexander counts inflexibility as an inherent cost of prewritten boxed text, since one passage must serve every approach and condition.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls', The Alexandrian, 2022
claims.quote: The result is inherently less flexible.
claims.page: GM Don't List #13, 'So why wouldn't you use boxed text?'

claims.claim: Justin Alexander names freeze-frame boxed text as the failure in which the world keeps moving while the characters stand frozen.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls', The Alexandrian, 2022
claims.quote: PCs are frozen in place while a bunch of stuff happens
claims.page: GM Don't List #13, 'Sins of the Box'

claims.claim: Justin Alexander names the reaction point as the place in a description past which the world must not move without the players.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls', The Alexandrian, 2022
claims.quote: What we’ve identified here is the reaction point
claims.page: GM Don't List #13, 'Sins of the Box'

claims.claim: Justin Alexander condemns remote-control boxed text, which declares the thoughts, feelings or actions of the player characters.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls', The Alexandrian, 2022
claims.quote: declaring the thoughts or feelings or (worse yet!) actions of the PCs

claims.claim: Justin Alexander's rule for read-aloud text is to show the scene and never to tell the players how they are reacting to it.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls', The Alexandrian, 2022
claims.quote: Don’t tell them how they’re reacting to it.

claims.claim: A reader commenting on the Alexandrian recalls a lost Wizards devblog article whose thesis was that GM description should never run past three sentences.
claims.source: Reader comment by 'mellonbread', 2 August 2022, on The Alexandrian
claims.quote: should never be longer than three sentences
